summary.title: Search for High-Energy Gamma-Ray Emission from Anomalous X-ray Pulsar, 4U 0142+61
summary.authors: Sinem Şaşmaz Müş and Ersin Göğüş
summary.executive_summary: Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated neutron stars powered by ultra-strong magnetic fields, and until 2004 they were known only as soft X-ray emitters. The discovery of a hard X-ray/soft gamma-ray component from several AXPs (1E 1841-045, 4U 0142+61, 1RXS J170849.0-400910) provided important insight but posed a serious challenge to explain its origin. The physical mechanism of the hard emission component has still not been fully resolved, motivating this work. This paper investigates the high-energy gamma-ray properties of the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, using data collected with the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on board Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to establish the spectral behavior of the source on a very broad energy span and search for pulsed emission. The LAT operates in the energy band of 20 MeV-300 GeV and has been operating as an all sky monitor since 2008 August 4. The authors accumulated LAT data within a 15° radius centered at 4U 0142+61, collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29 with an exposure time of ~31.7 Ms, and performed unbinned likelihood analysis using ScienceTools v9r15p2 with P6 V3 DIFFUSE as the instrumental response. They also employed contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations to obtain the spin ephemeris of the source, selecting 53 RXTE observations performed between 2008 August 4 and 2010 April 30 with a total exposure time of about 196 ks. The search for persistent emission yielded no significant detection: the Test Statistics (TS) value is ~0.23 for the 15° region (detection significance less than 1σ) and ~3 for the 2° region (detection significance less than 4σ). The 3σ flux upper limits with a power law index 2.5 are 2.32 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band and 1.28 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band. For pulsed emission, both LAT pulse profiles are consistent with random fluctuations with respect to its mean, and the 3σ upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band and 2.3% in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band. The lower energy LAT passband (30-200 MeV) also resulted with no evidence of pulsed emission; the 3σ RMS pulsed fraction upper limit is 1.6%. The authors constructed the νFν spectrum of the source in the 15 keV-10 GeV range by adopting the hard X-ray spectrum presented in den Hartog et al. (2008) and placing the upper limits calculated in this work. The upper limit curve is a power law with an index of -0.76, and these two curves intersect with each other at ~1.1 MeV, which is an upper limit to the spectral break energy. This estimate is in accordance with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007) and the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The main conclusion is that no significant high-energy gamma-ray emission is detected, but the obtained upper limits help constrain existing physical models. The results are important because our LAT upper limits are much lower than high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL (den Hartog et al. 2008).

The spectral break energy upper limit is consistent with the coronal emission model and the quantum electrodynamics model.

Executive Summary
Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated neutron stars powered by ultra-strong magnetic fields, and until 2004 they were known only as soft X-ray emitters. The discovery of a hard X-ray/soft gamma-ray component from several AXPs (1E 1841-045, 4U 0142+61, 1RXS J170849.0-400910) provided important insight but posed a serious challenge to explain its origin. The physical mechanism of the hard emission component has still not been fully resolved, motivating this work. This paper investigates the high-energy gamma-ray properties of the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, using data collected with the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on board Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to establish the spectral behavior of the source on a very broad energy span and search for pulsed emission. The LAT operates in the energy band of 20 MeV-300 GeV and has been operating as an all sky monitor since 2008 August 4. The authors accumulated LAT data within a 15° radius centered at 4U 0142+61, collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29 with an exposure time of ~31.7 Ms, and performed unbinned likelihood analysis using ScienceTools v9r15p2 with P6 V3 DIFFUSE as the instrumental response. They also employed contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations to obtain the spin ephemeris of the source, selecting 53 RXTE observations performed between 2008 August 4 and 2010 April 30 with a total exposure time of about 196 ks. The search for persistent emission yielded no significant detection: the Test Statistics (TS) value is ~0.23 for the 15° region (detection significance less than 1σ) and ~3 for the 2° region (detection significance less than 4σ). The 3σ flux upper limits with a power law index 2.5 are 2.32 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band and 1.28 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band. For pulsed emission, both LAT pulse profiles are consistent with random fluctuations with respect to its mean, and the 3σ upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band and 2.3% in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band. The lower energy LAT passband (30-200 MeV) also resulted with no evidence of pulsed emission; the 3σ RMS pulsed fraction upper limit is 1.6%. The authors constructed the νFν spectrum of the source in the 15 keV-10 GeV range by adopting the hard X-ray spectrum presented in den Hartog et al. (2008) and placing the upper limits calculated in this work. The upper limit curve is a power law with an index of -0.76, and these two curves intersect with each other at ~1.1 MeV, which is an upper limit to the spectral break energy. This estimate is in accordance with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007) and the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The main conclusion is that no significant high-energy gamma-ray emission is detected, but the obtained upper limits help constrain existing physical models. The results are important because our LAT upper limits are much lower than high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL (den Hartog et al. 2008).

Research Context
AXPs are intriguing sources since their discovery in early 80s. Until 2004, AXPs were known as strong emitters of soft X-rays only. The discovery of hard X-ray component from AXPs posed a serious challenge to explain its origin. The physical mechanism of the hard emission component has still not been fully resolved. AXPs are commonly regarded as young isolated neutron stars powered by extremely strong magnetic fields. Strong magnetic fields can efficiently slow these young systems down via magnetic breaking. Establishing spectral shapes on a wide energy range is crucial to understand the hard emission component. The LAT enables investigation of high-energy behavior of these sources with unprecedented data quality.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central goal is to investigate the high-energy gamma-ray properties of the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61. The study aims to establish the spectral behavior of the source on a very broad energy span. The study aims to search for pulsed emission from 4U 0142+61. The study presents results of detailed search for the persistent and pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission from 4U 0142+61. The predicted outcome is no significant detection, but upper limits to the persistent high-energy gamma-ray emission flux. The upper limits help constrain existing physical models of the hard emission component. The hard X-ray emission could originate from a plasma corona around the magnetar (Beloborodov & Thompson 2007). The fast-mode breakdown model (Heyl & Hernquist 2005a,b) predicts a break energy around 1 MeV. The upscattered surface thermal X-ray photons model (Baring & Harding 2007) is another attempt to explain the hard emission.

Methodological Details
The study uses LAT data on board Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The LAT operates in the energy band of 20 MeV-300 GeV. The LAT is a pair conversion telescope with a high-resolution silicon tracker, calorimeter, anticoincidence detector, programmable trigger and data acquisition system. The LAT has been operating as an all sky monitor in high-energy gamma-rays since 2008 August 4. The LAT covers the full sky in approximately every 3 hours. The LAT data were accumulated within a 15° radius centered at 4U 0142+61. The data were collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29. The exposure time is ~31.7 Ms. A 2° radius region around the source was used for spectral analysis to avoid contamination from nearby bright sources. The unbinned likelihood analysis used ScienceTools v9r15p2 with P6 V3 DIFFUSE as the instrumental response. The maximum zenith angle was set to 105° to eliminate background gamma-rays due to the Earth limb. The galactic diffuse emission was modeled with gll iem v02.fit.

Procedures And Architectures
The diffuse gamma-ray emission from the Milky Way was modeled with the latest model. The isotropic iem v02.txt was used to account for the extragalactic isotropic diffuse emission and residual instrumental background. The spectral fits and flux calculations were done with the python version of gtlike, pyLikelihood. Photon arrival times were converted to that at the solar system barycenter using gtbary of ScienceTools. The precise spin ephemeris was obtained using contemporaneous RXTE observations. Only the PCA observations were employed, sensitive to photon energies between 2-60 keV. 53 RXTE observations were selected performed between 2008 August 4 and 2010 April 30. The RXTE observations were performed under Program IDs P93019, P94019 and P05019. The total exposure time of all selected observations is about 196 ks. Events were extracted in the 2-10 keV range collected with the PCA. The arrival times were converted to the solar system barycenter using faxbary tool of HEASoft 6.8. A Fourier based epoch folding technique was used to obtain the spin ephemeris.

Key Results
4U 0142+61 is clearly not detected in the LAT energy passband. A point source search using the filtered event list with gtfindsrc yields no detection. The Test Statistics (TS) value is ~0.23 for the 15° region. The TS value of ~0.23 implies a detection significance less than 1σ. The 3σ flux upper limit in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band is 2.32 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The 3σ flux upper limit in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band is 1.28 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The spectral parameters and fluxes of the cataloged sources are consistent with the catalog values. The TS value is ~3 for the 2° region. The TS value of ~3 implies a detection significance less than 4σ. The 3σ upper limit in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band is 5.72 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The 3σ upper limit in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band is 1.29 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. Both LAT pulse profiles are consistent with random fluctuations with respect to its mean.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The upper limits help constrain existing physical models of the hard emission component. Our LAT upper limits are much lower than high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL. The spectral break upper limit is consistent with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007). Photons with energies in excess of ≳1 MeV would be trapped in the ultrastrong magnetic fields. The spectral break energy upper limit agrees with the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The excess optical emission in 4U 0142+61 places a constraint on the quantum electrodynamics model. The origin of the excess optical emission in 4U 0142+61 is not clear.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study reports no significant detection of high-energy gamma-ray emission. The origin of the excess optical emission in 4U 0142+61 is not clear. The constraint on the quantum electrodynamics model is not stringent. The study relies on contemporaneous RXTE observations to obtain the spin ephemeris.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the detailed search for persistent and pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission from 4U 0142+61. 2. The strongest evidence is the 3σ upper limits to the persistent high-energy gamma-ray emission flux. 3. The future path is to constrain existing physical models of the hard emission component.
